claim: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria is a permeability barrier to antibiotics and other cytotoxic agents, such as detergents.
source: The outer membrane (OM) of Gram-negative bacteria is a permeability barrier to antibiotics and other cytotoxic agents, such as detergents (Nikaido, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nikaido, 2003

claim: The outer membrane has a distinctive asymmetrical bilayer populated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet and phospholipids in the inner leaflet.
source: A key feature of the OM is its distinctive asymmetrical bilayer populated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet and phospholipids in the inner leaflet (Funahara and Nikaido, 1980; Kamio and Nikaido, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to Funahara and Nikaido, 1980; Kamio and Nikaido, 1976

claim: Lateral interactions between LPS molecules mediated by divalent cations on the surface and packing of hydrocarbon chains in the membrane impede the passage of both hydrophilic and large hydrophobic molecules.
source: Lateral interactions between LPS molecules mediated by divalent cations on the surface and packing of hydrocarbon chains in the membrane impede the passage of both hydrophilic and large hydrophobic molecules (Nikaido, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nikaido, 2003

claim: LPS is composed of a conserved lipid A molecule, a core oligosaccharide, and a variable O-antigen glycan.
source: LPS is composed of a conserved lipid A molecule, a core oligosaccharide, and a variable O-antigen glycan.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about LPS structure

claim: Lipid A is synthesized in the cytoplasm where the core oligosaccharide is attached to form core-LPS.
source: Lipid A is synthesized in the cytoplasm where the core oligosaccharide is attached to form core-LPS (Whitfield and Trent, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitfield and Trent, 2014

claim: Core-LPS is flipped into the periplasmic space by the inner membrane ATPase MsbA.
source: This molecule is flipped into the periplasmic space by the inner membrane ATPase MsbA (Ho et al., 2018; Mi et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ho et al., 2018; Mi et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 1998

claim: The O-antigen is appended onto core-LPS in the periplasm and LPS is transported to the outer leaflet of the OM by the LPS transport (Lpt) system.
source: The O-antigen is appended onto core-LPS in the periplasm and LPS is transported to the outer leaflet of the OM by the LPS transport (Lpt) system (Abeyrathne et al., 2005; Han et al., 2012; Okuda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abeyrathne et al., 2005; Han et al., 2012; Okuda et al., 2016

claim: In E. coli, all 7 components of the Lpt pathway, LptABCDEFG, are essential and shuttle LPS molecules from the IM across the periplasm to the OM.
source: In E. coli, all 7 components of the Lpt pathway, LptABCDEFG, are essential and shuttle LPS molecules from the IM across the periplasm to the OM (Okuda et al., 2016; Okuda et al., 2012; Ruiz et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okuda et al., 2016; Okuda et al., 2012; Ruiz et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2006

claim: LptD is a β-barrel outer membrane protein (OMP) responsible for the final unidirectional insertion of LPS into the OM outer leaflet.
source: LptD is a β-barrel outer membrane protein (OMP) responsible for the final unidirectional insertion of LPS into the OM outer leaflet (Botos et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Botos et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015

claim: The LptD β-barrel is comprised of 26 anti-parallel β-strands with a proposed lateral gate formed where the first and last β-strands interact.
source: The LptD β-barrel is comprised of 26 anti-parallel β-strands with a proposed lateral gate formed where the first and last β-strands interact (Dong et al., 2014; Qiao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2014; Qiao et al., 2014

claim: LptD possesses long extracellular, environmentally-exposed loops and short periplasmic loops connecting adjacent strands.
source: Like other Gram-negative β-barrel OMPs, LptD possess long extracellular, environmentally-exposed loops and short periplasmic loops connecting adjacent strands (Franklin and Slusky, 2018; Rollauer et al., 2015; Schulz, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Franklin and Slusky, 2018; Rollauer et al., 2015; Schulz, 2002

claim: LptD forms an obligate interaction with the OM lipoprotein LptE.
source: LptD forms an obligate interaction with the OM lipoprotein LptE (Chimalakonda et al., 2011; Freinkman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chimalakonda et al., 2011; Freinkman et al., 2011

claim: An N-terminal jelly roll domain is located on the periplasmic side of the β-barrel below the lateral gate.
source: An N-terminal jelly roll domain is located on the periplasmic side of the β-barrel below the lateral gate.
evidence: Stated as structural feature of LptD

claim: The hydrophobic lipid A portion of LPS is embedded in the hydrophobic jelly roll domain.
source: Structural, biochemical, and genetic analyses suggest that the hydrophobic lipid A portion of LPS is embedded in the hydrophobic jelly roll domain.
evidence: Based on structural, biochemical, and genetic analyses

claim: The presumed model for LPS transport across the OM posits that lipid A is inserted into the hydrophobic OM through a lateral gate of LptD.
source: The presumed model for LPS transport across the OM posits that lipid A is inserted into the hydrophobic OM through a lateral gate of LptD (Botos et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Botos et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015

claim: The polar sugars of the LPS core oligosaccharide and O-antigen are presumably moved through the LptD β-barrel lumen and flipped to the exterior of the cell by an unknown mechanism.
source: By an unknown mechanism, the polar sugars of the LPS core oligosaccharide and O-antigen are presumably moved through the LptD β-barrel lumen and flipped to the exterior of the cell.
evidence: Stated as presumed mechanism with unknown details

claim: LptD represents a potential new antibacterial target due to its essential role in OM biogenesis, high conservation among Gram-negative bacteria, and exposure to the extracellular environment.
source: Due to its essential role in OM biogenesis, high conservation among Gram-negative bacteria, and exposure to the extracellular environment, LptD represents a potential new antibacterial target.
evidence: Logical inference based on stated properties of LptD

claim: Crosslinking LPS to LptD in the jelly roll domain or the lateral gate inhibits growth.
source: Genetic experiments show that crosslinking LPS to LptD in the jelly roll domain or the lateral gate, or introduction of disulfide bonds that disrupt the proposed LPS path through LptD, inhibit growth (Gu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015

claim: Introduction of disulfide bonds that disrupt the proposed LPS path through LptD inhibits growth.
source: Genetic experiments show that crosslinking LPS to LptD in the jelly roll domain or the lateral gate, or introduction of disulfide bonds that disrupt the proposed LPS path through LptD, inhibit growth (Gu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015

claim: Two antibacterial peptides targeting LptD have been described, both presumably targeting the periplasmic jelly roll domain.
source: Indeed, two antibacterial peptides targeting LptD have been described, both presumably targeting the periplasmic jelly roll domain (Srinivas et al., 2010; Vetterli et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Srinivas et al., 2010; Vetterli et al., 2018

claim: Removal of the LptD extracellular loop 4 (L4), imp4213, disrupts the OM barrier leading to sensitization to antibiotics.
source: For example, removal of the LptD extracellular loop 4 (L4), imp4213, is known to disrupt the OM barrier leading to sensitization to antibiotics (Sampson et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sampson et al., 1989

claim: The roles of the extracellular LptD loops remain largely underexplored due to a lack of robust tools to systematically assess structure-function relationships in the context of a native OM.
source: However, the roles of the extracellular LptD loops remain largely underexplored due to a lack of robust tools to systematically assess structure-function relationships in the context of a native OM.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field

claim: Four diverse strategies were pursued to produce thousands of mAbs that bound to LptD.
source: Accordingly, here we pursued four diverse strategies to produce thousands of mAbs that bound to LptD.
evidence: Description of experimental approach in the study

claim: The study constructed a diverse library of >3000 monoclonal antibodies to assess the roles of extracellular loops (ECLs) in LptD.
source: We constructed a diverse library of >3000 monoclonal antibodies to assess the roles of extracellular loops (ECLs) in LptD, an essential OMP that inserts lipopolysaccharide into the outer membrane of Escherichia coli.
evidence: Description of experimental work performed in the study

claim: Epitope binning and mapping experiments with LptD-loop-deletion mutants demonstrated that 7 of the 13 ECLs are targeted by antibodies.
source: Epitope binning and mapping experiments with LptD-loop-deletion mutants demonstrated that 7 of the 13 ECLs are targeted by antibodies.
evidence: Results from epitope binning and mapping experiments in the study

claim: Only ECLs inaccessible to antibodies were required for the structure or function of LptD.
source: Only ECLs inaccessible to antibodies were required for the structure or function of LptD.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental results in the study

claim: Antibody-accessible loops evolved to protect key extracellular regions of LptD, but are themselves dispensable.
source: Our results suggest that antibody-accessible loops evolved to protect key extracellular regions of LptD, but are themselves dispensable.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results

claim: No α-LptD antibody interfered with essential functions of LptD.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, no α-LptD antibody interfered with essential functions of LptD.
evidence: Experimental result from antibody functional testing

claim: The discovery campaigns generated more than 7000 hybridomas and more than 3,000 ELISA+ LptD-specific mAbs.
source: Cumulatively, the discovery campaigns generated more than 7000 hybridomas and more than 3,000 ELISA+ LptD-specific mAbs (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from antibody discovery campaigns shown in Figure 1C

claim: 774 ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs from the peptide and protein rat immunizations were purified.
source: In total, 774 ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs from the peptide and protein rat immunizations, 952 ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs from the mouse immunizations, and 1494 α-LptD mAbs from the targeted boost-and-sort immunizations were purified (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from antibody purification shown in Figure 1C

claim: 952 ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs from the mouse immunizations were purified.
source: In total, 774 ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs from the peptide and protein rat immunizations, 952 ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs from the mouse immunizations, and 1494 α-LptD mAbs from the targeted boost-and-sort immunizations were purified (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from antibody purification shown in Figure 1C

claim: 1494 α-LptD mAbs from the targeted boost-and-sort immunizations were purified.
source: In total, 774 ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs from the peptide and protein rat immunizations, 952 ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs from the mouse immunizations, and 1494 α-LptD mAbs from the targeted boost-and-sort immunizations were purified (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from antibody purification shown in Figure 1C

claim: 9–30% of the ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs were FACS+ on E. coli ΔwaaD, depending on the immunization campaign.
source: Depending on the immunization campaign, 9–30% of the ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs were FACS+ on E. coli ΔwaaD, while <1% of the same antibodies were FACS+ on E. coli K-12 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data from FACS assays shown in Figure 2A

claim: <1% of the ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs were FACS+ on E. coli K-12.
source: Depending on the immunization campaign, 9–30% of the ELISA+ α-LptD mAbs were FACS+ on E. coli ΔwaaD, while <1% of the same antibodies were FACS+ on E. coli K-12 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data from FACS assays shown in Figure 2A

claim: The E. coli K-12 FACS+ α-LptD mAbs were a subset of all the FACS+ mAbs, binding equally well to E. coli K-12 and E. coli ΔwaaD cells.
source: The E. coli K-12 FACS+ α-LptD mAbs were a subset of all the FACS+ mAbs, binding equally well to E. coli K-12 and E. coli ΔwaaD cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and were discovered in both mouse and rat immunization campaigns.
evidence: Experimental data from FACS assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: LPS presents a significant barrier to accessing surface epitopes on E. coli.
source: These results reinforce the finding that LPS presents a significant barrier to accessing surface epitopes on E. coli (Bentley and Klebba, 1988; Storek et al., 2018) and suggest that the ECLs of OMPs may be masked or intimately associated with the core sugars of the LPS.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bentley and Klebba, 1988; Storek et al., 2018 and experimental data

claim: The ECLs of OMPs may be masked or intimately associated with the core sugars of the LPS.
source: These results reinforce the finding that LPS presents a significant barrier to accessing surface epitopes on E. coli (Bentley and Klebba, 1988; Storek et al., 2018) and suggest that the ECLs of OMPs may be masked or intimately associated with the core sugars of the LPS.
evidence: Inference from experimental results

source: ELISAs were performed with 134 FACS+ and 233 FACS- α-LptD mAbs using purified LptDE protein from two closely related Enterobacteriaceae species, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Enterobacter cloacae, which share 82% and 84% overall protein identity and 71% and 76% identify between the ECLs only when compared with E. coli LptD, respectively (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: E. cloacae LptD shares 84% overall protein identity with E. coli LptD.
source: ELISAs were performed with 134 FACS+ and 233 FACS- α-LptD mAbs using purified LptDE protein from two closely related Enterobacteriaceae species, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Enterobacter cloacae, which share 82% and 84% overall protein identity and 71% and 76% identify between the ECLs only when compared with E. coli LptD, respectively (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

evidence: Sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: The majority of FACS+ (61%) α-LptD mAbs bound only E. coli LptDE by ELISA.
source: The majority of FACS+ (61%) and FACS- (69%) α-LptD mAbs bound only E. coli LptDE by ELISA (Figure 2C).

claim: The majority of FACS- (69%) α-LptD mAbs bound only E. coli LptDE by ELISA.
source: The majority of FACS+ (61%) and FACS- (69%) α-LptD mAbs bound only E. coli LptDE by ELISA (Figure 2C).

claim: 10 (7%) α-LptD mAbs bound to LptDE from all three species (E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and E. cloacae).
source: Indeed, we identified 10 (7%) α-LptD mAbs that bound to LptDE from all three species and 42 that bound either E. coli plus K. pneumoniae (22%) or E. coli plus E. cloacae (9%) LptDE (Figure 2C).

claim: 42 α-LptD mAbs bound either E. coli plus K. pneumoniae (22%) or E. coli plus E. cloacae (9%) LptDE.
source: Indeed, we identified 10 (7%) α-LptD mAbs that bound to LptDE from all three species and 42 that bound either E. coli plus K. pneumoniae (22%) or E. coli plus E. cloacae (9%) LptDE (Figure 2C).

claim: Two major epitope bins and a possible third bin with limited overlap were identified from the FACS+ α-LptD mAbs.
source: We identified two major epitope bins and a possible third bin with limited overlap (Figure 2D).
evidence: Results from SPR-based epitope binning shown in Figure 2D

claim: Most three-species cross-reactive α-LptD mAbs were tightly clustered in the epitope map.
source: When the species cross-reactivity data were considered, most three-species cross-reactive α-LptD mAbs were tightly clustered, while those that bound only E. coli LptDE formed a distinct cluster (Figure 2D).

claim: α-LptD mAbs that bound only E. coli LptDE formed a distinct cluster in the epitope map.
source: When the species cross-reactivity data were considered, most three-species cross-reactive α-LptD mAbs were tightly clustered, while those that bound only E. coli LptDE formed a distinct cluster (Figure 2D).
evidence: Results from epitope binning analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: 13 lptD mutants were constructed, each lacking the region encoding one of the 13 ECLs.
source: We constructed 13 lptD mutants, each lacking the region encoding one of the 13 ECLs (Figure 3A).
evidence: Description of experimental construction shown in Figure 3A

claim: In the presence of arabinose, which induces a chromosomal wild-type lptD, all strains grew.
source: In the presence of arabinose, which induces a chromosomal wild-type lptD, all strains grew (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental growth data shown in Figure 3B

claim: In the absence of arabinose, all lptD loop mutants supported growth in the K-12 strain with the exception of loop 2 (L2) removal, which showed reduced growth.
source: In the absence of arabinose, all lptD loop mutants supported growth in the K-12 strain with the exception of loop 2 (L2) removal, which showed reduced growth (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental growth data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The levels of the LptD loop deletion protein produced were similar to the protein level of wild-type LptD in all cases when growth was observed.
source: In all cases when growth was observed, the levels of the LptD loop deletion protein produced were similar to the protein level of wild-type LptD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: LptD is highly tolerable to genetic manipulation of its ECLs.
source: Thus, LptD is highly tolerable to genetic manipulation of its ECLs.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental growth data of loop deletion mutants

claim: In the E. coli ΔwaaD background, LptD lacking either loop 2 or loop 10 were unable to support bacterial growth on solid growth agar.
source: In the E. coli ΔwaaD background, LptD lacking either loop 2 or loop 10 were unable to support bacterial growth on solid growth agar (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental growth data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Loop 10 is important for LptD folding or activity in the E. coli ΔwaaD strain.
source: The inability of LptD lacking L10 (LptDΔL10) to support growth of the E. coli ΔwaaD strain suggested that this ECL is important for LptD folding or activity in this strain.
evidence: Inference from experimental growth data

claim: LptDΔL10 was produced and did support growth of E. coli K-12.
source: In contrast, the LptDΔL10 variant was produced and did support growth of E. coli K-12 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that LptDΔL10 was folded and sufficiently functional in the strain producing core-LPS but not the minimal LPS of E. coli ΔwaaD strain.
evidence: Experimental growth and Western blot data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: LptDΔL10 was folded and sufficiently functional in the strain producing core-LPS but not the minimal LPS of E. coli ΔwaaD strain.
source: In contrast, the LptDΔL10 variant was produced and did support growth of E. coli K-12 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that LptDΔL10 was folded and sufficiently functional in the strain producing core-LPS but not the minimal LPS of E. coli ΔwaaD strain.
evidence: Inference from experimental growth data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: In the E. coli K-12 strain, LptDΔL10 grew at a decreased rate.
source: In the absence of arabinose, the E. coli K-12 strain producing LptDΔL10 grew, but at a decreased rate, and the strain with LptDΔL2 exhibited a dramatically prolonged lag phase and severe growth phenotype (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Experimental growth curve data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1

claim: The E. coli K-12 strain with LptDΔL2 exhibited a dramatically prolonged lag phase and severe growth phenotype.
source: In the absence of arabinose, the E. coli K-12 strain producing LptDΔL10 grew, but at a decreased rate, and the strain with LptDΔL2 exhibited a dramatically prolonged lag phase and severe growth phenotype (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Experimental growth curve data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1

claim: E. coli ΔwaaD expressing LptDΔL10 did not grow at all.
source: In contrast, E. coli ΔwaaD expressing LptDΔL10 did not grow at all, but expression of LptDΔL2 supported growth in liquid media (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Experimental growth curve data shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1

claim: E. coli ΔwaaD expressing LptDΔL2 supported growth in liquid media.
source: In contrast, E. coli ΔwaaD expressing LptDΔL10 did not grow at all, but expression of LptDΔL2 supported growth in liquid media (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Experimental growth curve data shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1

claim: L2 and L10 are important for LptD folding, activity, interaction with the β-barrel assembly machinery component BamA, or a combination of these.
source: Thus, L2 and L10 are important for LptD folding, activity, interaction with the β-barrel assembly machinery component BamA, or a combination of these.

claim: The LptDΔL10 loop deletion mutant was better tolerated in E. coli K-12 compared to the LPS-truncated ΔwaaD strain while in liquid growth media.
source: Also, the LptDΔL10 loop deletion mutant was better tolerated in E. coli K-12 compared to the LPS-truncated ΔwaaD strain while in liquid growth media the LptDΔL2 mutant is better tolerated in the E. coli ΔwaaD strain.
evidence: Comparison of experimental growth data

claim: The LptDΔL2 mutant is better tolerated in the E. coli ΔwaaD strain in liquid growth media.
source: Also, the LptDΔL10 loop deletion mutant was better tolerated in E. coli K-12 compared to the LPS-truncated ΔwaaD strain while in liquid growth media the LptDΔL2 mutant is better tolerated in the E. coli ΔwaaD strain.
evidence: Comparison of experimental growth data

claim: This result is consistent with the synthetic lethality of other mutations that affect OM biogenesis, specifically bam101, ΔbamB, ΔsurA, and ΔlpxL, in LPS-truncated E. coli strain backgrounds.
source: This result is consistent with the synthetic lethality of other mutations that affect OM biogenesis, specifically bam101, ΔbamB, ΔsurA, and ΔlpxL, in LPS-truncated E. coli strain backgrounds (Klein et al., 2009; Storek et al., 2019) highlighting the redundancy that exists to maintain this important barrier structure.

claim: The minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of both rifampicin and vancomycin were lower for strains producing LptDΔL2, LptDΔL8, and LptDΔL10 indicating an OM defect.
